title: Contact Center — Helping the Public by Phone, Chat, Email, and the Web
description: U.S. federal contact center blueprint: one mission with the outcomes it seeks and ways to measure them, ten capabilities from planning the service to reporting on it, with their reference requirements, example implementation patterns with their tradeoffs, and discovery question sets for contact center results and for contact center operations. It follows the Government Service Delivery Improvement Act, OMB Circular A-11 Section 280, the 21st Century IDEA, and Sections 504 and 508 of the Rehabilitation Act, and builds on Common Capabilities for case management, records, identity and access, data protection, and security logging.
jurisdictions: United States — federal agencies that answer the public by phone, chat, email, and the web

sources.title: 5 U.S.C. §§ 321–324 — Government service delivery (Government Service Delivery Improvement Act)
sources.note: Enacted in Public Law 118-231. OMB’s Federal Government Service Delivery Lead sets governmentwide standards for service delivery that weigh ease, efficiency, transparency, accessibility, fairness, burden, and duration, including wait and processing times, and collects and reports data on service delivery (§ 322). Each agency head names a senior official who coordinates service delivery improvements across the agency’s channels and uses that data to improve them (§ 323).

sources.title: OMB Circular A-11 (2025), Section 280 — Managing Customer Experience and Improving Service Delivery
sources.note: Carries out the Government Service Delivery Improvement Act. High Impact Service Providers designate priority services each year, deploy at least one post-transaction customer feedback survey for each, following OMB’s question wording and response choices, and submit the data to OMB by the final business day of January, April, July, and October for publication (§§ 280.4–280.6). Surveys are approved under the Paperwork Reduction Act through a Section 280 umbrella clearance (§ 280.7).

sources.title: Performance.gov — Customer feedback data handbook
sources.note: The Section 280 survey: a trust question, such as “This interaction increased my trust in [agency],” and drivers people choose from, including effectiveness (“My issue was resolved”), ease (“It was easy to find what I needed”), efficiency, transparency, fairness, and employee helpfulness. Trust is the share of positive answers, with a benchmark of 75 percent or higher, and results are published on performance.gov.

sources.title: 21st Century Integrated Digital Experience Act (21st Century IDEA), Public Law 115-336
sources.note: New or redesigned websites and digital services are, to the greatest extent practicable, accessible under Section 508, consistent, searchable, secure, designed around user needs, and usable on mobile devices (§ 3). Agencies make services available digitally, and maintain an accessible way to complete digital services in person, on paper, or by other means, so people aren’t kept from them (§ 4).

sources.title: 29 U.S.C. § 794 — Nondiscrimination under Federal grants and programs (Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act)
sources.note: No qualified individual with a disability may, because of the disability, be excluded from, denied the benefits of, or discriminated against under any program or activity conducted by an executive agency. Each agency issues its own rules for the programs it conducts.

sources.title: 28 CFR § 39.160 — Communications (Department of Justice, Section 504 in federally conducted programs)
sources.note: The Justice Department’s rule, which other agencies’ Section 504 rules follow closely. The agency takes appropriate steps to communicate effectively with applicants, participants, and the public, provides auxiliary aids where necessary, giving primary consideration to the person’s request, and where it communicates by telephone, uses TDDs or equally effective telecommunication systems.

sources.title: U.S. Access Board — Revised Section 508 Standards, 36 CFR Part 1194
sources.note: Information and communication technology that agencies buy, build, maintain, or use conforms to the standards (E201.1). For two-way voice communication, voice mail, auto-attendant, interactive voice response, and caller identification systems are usable with a TTY (412.8.4), and caller identification is visible and audible (412.6). Web content and software conform to WCAG 2.0 Level AA.

sources.title: Section508.gov — Annual Section 508 assessment
sources.note: Under Section 508 as the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 amended it, agencies respond each year to OMB’s criteria for assessing their Section 508 compliance, and GSA reports the results to Congress.

sources.title: Executive Order 14224 — Designating English as the Official Language of the United States (March 1, 2025)
sources.note: Revokes Executive Order 13166 on access to services for people with limited English proficiency, while saying nothing in the order requires a change in agencies’ services. Agency heads decide what their missions need, and aren’t required to stop documents or services offered in other languages (§ 3(b)).

sources.title: Plain Writing Act of 2010, Public Law 111-274
sources.note: Each agency uses plain writing, clear, concise, and well organized, in every covered document it issues or substantially revises (§ 4(b)). Covered documents include letters, publications, forms, notices, and instructions necessary for obtaining a federal benefit or service (§ 3(2)).

sources.title: 44 U.S.C. § 3502 — Definitions (Paperwork Reduction Act)
sources.note: A collection of information includes answers to identical questions posed to ten or more people outside the federal government, which needs OMB approval under the Paperwork Reduction Act before it’s used.

sources.title: 5 U.S.C. § 552a — Records maintained on individuals (Privacy Act of 1974)
sources.note: An agency discloses a record from a system of records only with the person’s written request or consent, or under a listed exception (b). It tells people it asks for information the authority, purpose, routine uses, and effect of not answering (e)(3), keeps safeguards for the records (e)(10), and sets in its rules the requirements for identifying a person who asks for their own record (f)(2).

sources.title: National Archives — General Records Schedule 6.5, Public Customer Service Records
sources.note: Covers records of call and service centers that serve the public by phone, chat, and email, including incoming requests and responses, tracking logs, recordings used for quality control and training, FAQs, reports, and customer feedback and surveys: destroy 1 year after resolved, or when no longer needed for business use (item 010). Centers that take tips or allegations for oversight and enforcement offices need their own schedule.

sources.title: OMB Memorandum M-25-21 — Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust (April 3, 2025)
sources.note: Agencies inventory their AI use cases. AI whose output is a principal basis for decisions with a significant effect on rights or safety is high-impact, and uses affecting the ability to apply for, or eligibility for, critical federal services and benefits are presumed to be. High-impact uses need pre-deployment testing, an impact assessment, ongoing monitoring, trained operators, human oversight, timely human review and appeal, and a way for the public to give feedback (§ 4(b)).

sources.title: NIST — Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
sources.note: A framework for voluntary use in managing the risks of AI systems, built around four functions, govern, map, measure, and manage, and the characteristics of trustworthy AI, such as being valid, accountable, and fair.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63-4 — Digital Identity Guidelines
sources.note: Requirements for identity proofing, authenticators, and authentication for people who use government systems, including the people signing in to an agency’s public website.

sources.title: GSA Contact Center Center of Excellence — Fifteen Plays of Our Contact Center Approach (2020)
sources.note: Practices for modernizing federal contact centers, including workforce management against the center’s service-level standard, assessing whether calls and emails are answered soon enough, training that raises first-call resolution, evaluating agents, and building one shared knowledge base so answers are consistent.

sources.title: Digital.gov — Contact center technologies
sources.note: The technologies a contact center commonly runs on, including automatic call distribution, intelligent routing, interactive voice response, web chat, email response management, knowledge management, TTY services, and workforce management.

elements.title: Contact Center
elements.description: Help members of the public get answers and get things done with the agency, by phone, chat, email, and the web: reach them without a long wait, resolve what they came for on the first contact where possible, serve people with disabilities as well as anyone, protect what they share, and use what they say to improve the agency’s services.

attributes.tagline: Helping the public by phone, chat, email, and the web
principles: Each contact is one record, with its channel, its reason, the answer, and any handoff
People can move from the web to chat to a call without starting over
Agents, the website, and virtual agents draw on the same approved answers
People who call through relay or TTY, or use a screen reader, get the same service as anyone else
No one has to use the web to get help; a person is always reachable
A short survey after each contact goes back to the teams that can fix the cause
AI answers routine questions and suggests answers to agents, and people decide anything about a person’s case

elements.title: People reach help without a long wait
elements.description: Calls are answered, chats are picked up, and emails get a reply within the times the agency sets, even on its busiest days.

measures.title: Average speed of answer
measures.description: The average time callers wait for an agent after choosing to speak to one, and the average time to a first reply on chat and email, by channel and by month. Most contact center systems report these figures already.

measures.title: Contacts abandoned while waiting
measures.description: The share of calls and chats in which the person gave up before reaching an agent, by channel and by hour, which shows when staffing falls short.

elements.title: People get what they came for on the first contact
elements.description: Agents and self-service give correct, complete answers, so people don’t have to call back, try another channel, or be passed from office to office.

measures.title: First contact resolution
measures.description: The share of contacts resolved without the person contacting the agency again about the same matter within a set period, such as seven days, as the center defines it.

measures.title: People who say their issue was resolved
measures.description: The share of post-contact survey respondents who choose “My issue was resolved,” the effectiveness driver in OMB’s Section 280 survey.

elements.title: Everyone can get help, whatever their abilities
elements.description: People who are deaf, hard of hearing, blind, or have other disabilities reach the center and are served as effectively as anyone else, on every channel the center offers.

measures.title: Public channels tested for Section 508 conformance
measures.description: The share of the center’s phone menus, chat, web forms, and virtual agents tested for conformance in the past year, and the open defects found, which feed the agency’s annual Section 508 assessment to OMB and GSA.

elements.title: People can find answers on their own
elements.description: Clear answers on the website, in the phone menu, and from virtual agents let people do routine things themselves, so agents have time for those who need a person.

measures.title: Contacts resolved in self-service
measures.description: The share of web, phone menu, and virtual agent sessions that end with an answer and no handoff to an agent or follow-up contact within a set period.

measures.title: People who say it was easy to find what they needed
measures.description: The share of post-contact survey respondents who choose the ease driver in OMB’s Section 280 survey, “It was easy to find what I needed.”

elements.title: What people share is protected
elements.description: The center discusses a person’s records only with that person, once they’ve been verified, or as the law allows, and keeps recordings and contact records only as long as their schedule allows.

measures.title: Privacy incidents that began in the contact center
measures.description: The number of privacy incidents that began with a contact, such as a record discussed with someone who wasn’t verified, from the agency’s privacy incident reports.

elements.title: What people say improves the service
elements.description: The center asks people about their experience after each contact, and the agency acts on what they say and on the reasons they contacted it in the first place.

measures.title: Trust after a contact
measures.description: The share of post-contact survey respondents who agree the interaction increased their trust in the agency, from OMB’s Section 280 survey. OMB’s benchmark is 75 percent or higher.

elements.title: The service’s results are open to view
elements.description: The agency reports what people say about its designated services to OMB each quarter, for publication on performance.gov, and shares its own service figures with the public.

measures.title: Quarterly feedback reported on time
measures.description: For services designated by a High Impact Service Provider, the quarters in which the agency sent its post-contact survey data to OMB by the final business day of January, April, July, and October.

elements.title: Service Planning & Staffing
elements.description: Ability to set standards for how long people wait on each channel, forecast contacts by channel, topic, and hour, schedule and train enough agents to meet the standards, and plan for surges such as deadlines, outages, and emergencies.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Many agencies contract for some or all of their agents, so the contract’s service levels become the standards the center is held to. Surges often follow the agency’s own deadlines and announcements, which program offices can warn the center about.

elements.title: Knowledge Management
elements.description: Ability to keep one approved set of answers that agents, the website, the phone menu, and virtual agents all use, written in plain language, each with an owner in the program office and a date for its next review.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Program offices own what an answer says; the center owns how it’s written and found. Each language the agency chooses to serve needs its own approved answers, kept in step with the English ones.

elements.title: Contact Intake & Routing
elements.description: Ability to take contacts by phone, chat, email, web form, and relay service, and send each to self-service or to an agent with the right skills, by topic and urgency, offering a callback instead of a long hold.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Some agencies run one center for everything; others have a center for each program, behind one number or several. Inventorying every number and inbox the public uses is often the first step.

elements.title: Self-Service & Virtual Assistants
elements.description: Ability to let people find answers and do routine things on their own, such as checking a status or updating an address, on the website, in the phone menu, or with a virtual agent, and to reach a person whenever they need one.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Which tasks suit self-service depends on the program and on what its systems can safely do without a person. An AI that only answers general questions is used differently from one that helps decide a person’s access to a benefit, which OMB presumes to be high-impact.

elements.title: Caller Verification
elements.description: Ability to confirm who someone is before discussing or changing their records, with steps matched to what’s at stake, and to record how each person was verified.
elements.applicabilityNotes: General questions need no verification. How much proof is enough for a status check, a change of address, or a payment question is set in the agency’s Privacy Act rules and its own risk decisions.

elements.title: Accessible Service
elements.description: Ability to serve people with disabilities as effectively as anyone else, taking relay and TTY calls, making phone menus, chat, and web forms work with assistive technology, and providing other aids when they’re needed, and to serve people in the other languages the agency chooses to support.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Each agency has its own Section 504 rule for the programs it conducts, like the Justice Department’s. Executive Order 14224 of March 2025 revoked Executive Order 13166 on limited English proficiency, so whether and in which languages the center serves people is now each agency’s decision, unless a program’s own law requires it.

elements.title: Contact Resolution & Handoff
elements.description: Ability to resolve each contact or, when a program office must act, hand it off as a case with everything already gathered, so the person doesn’t have to explain again, and to tell them what happens next and when.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Agents can often resolve general questions, while anything about a person’s case is decided by the program office. Where the line falls, and what an agent may change, is set for each program.

elements.title: Quality Review & Coaching
elements.description: Ability to review a sample of each agent’s calls, chats, and emails against a written standard, coach agents on what the reviews find, and fix wrong or unclear answers in the knowledge base.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Where agents work for a contractor, the contractor usually runs the reviews and the agency checks a sample of its own. Reviewers from the program offices help on topics agents often get wrong.

elements.title: Customer Feedback
elements.description: Ability to ask people about their experience right after a contact, using OMB’s Section 280 questions with the clearance the Paperwork Reduction Act requires, and send what they say to the teams that can fix the cause.
elements.applicabilityNotes: High Impact Service Providers must survey their designated services this way. Other offices can use the same questions and their department’s umbrella clearance, which lets their results be compared.

elements.title: Service Performance Reporting
elements.description: Ability to report the center’s waits, resolution, and feedback to managers and program offices, find the top reasons people contact the agency and where they get stuck, and send survey data to OMB each quarter for designated services.
elements.applicabilityNotes: Quarterly reporting to OMB applies to High Impact Service Providers’ designated services. The reasons people contact the agency are often the most useful figures for program offices, since they show what to fix upstream.

elements.title: Set wait and response standards for each channel, and measure against them
elements.description: Decide how long people should wait for an agent, a chat reply, and an email answer, and measure each channel against those standards, as the governmentwide service delivery standards weigh duration, including wait and processing times.

elements.title: Write public answers in plain language
elements.description: Write the answers, letters, and web content people need to get a benefit or service so they’re clear, concise, and well organized, as the Plain Writing Act requires of every covered document the agency issues or substantially revises.

elements.title: Give each answer an owner and a review date
elements.description: Name the program office that owns each approved answer, review it on a schedule and whenever the program changes, and take it down when it’s no longer right.

elements.title: Keep a way to get help without the web
elements.description: Keep an accessible way, such as by phone, on paper, or in person, to complete each service the agency offers online, so no one is kept from it for lack of digital access or skills.

elements.title: Build web and chat channels to the 21st Century IDEA’s standards
elements.description: Make each new or redesigned website, web form, and digital service accessible under Section 508, consistent in appearance, searchable, secure, designed around users’ needs, and usable on common mobile devices.

elements.title: Review each use of AI, and meet OMB’s practices for high-impact uses
elements.description: List each AI use, such as a virtual agent or suggested answers, in the agency’s AI use case inventory, and before deploying a high-impact use, test it, assess its impact, monitor it, train the staff who oversee it, and give people a timely human review and a chance to appeal.

elements.title: Confirm who a person is before discussing their records
elements.description: Disclose a record from a system of records only to the person it’s about, once they’ve met the identification requirements in the agency’s Privacy Act rules, or to others only with their written consent or as the Privacy Act allows.

elements.title: Communicate as effectively with people with disabilities as with others
elements.description: Take relay and TTY calls, or use equally effective systems, wherever the center talks with people by phone, and provide other aids people need, giving primary consideration to what each person asks for.

elements.title: Make phone menus and voice mail usable with a TTY
elements.description: Make the center’s voice mail, auto-attendant, interactive voice response, and caller identification usable with a TTY, as the Section 508 standards require of two-way voice systems.

elements.title: Make chat, web forms, and virtual agents conform to Section 508
elements.description: Buy, build, and keep the center’s digital channels conforming to the Section 508 standards, so people using screen readers, keyboards, magnification, or captions can use them, and test them before launch and after changes.

elements.title: Record each contact, and keep the records on schedule
elements.description: Record each contact’s reason, answer, and any handoff, and keep contact records, recordings, and survey data as General Records Schedule 6.5 allows, destroying them 1 year after the contact is resolved or when no longer needed for business use.

elements.title: Tell people why the center asks for their information
elements.description: Where the center asks people for information that goes into a system of records, such as on a web form or in chat, tell them the authority for asking, the purpose, the routine uses, and what happens if they don’t answer.

elements.title: Hand off with what’s been gathered, and say what happens next
elements.description: When a program office must act, send it the contact’s details so the person doesn’t have to repeat them, and tell the person who will act, what they’ll need, and when to expect an answer.

elements.title: Review a sample of each agent’s contacts against a written standard
elements.description: Score a regular sample of each agent’s calls, chats, and emails against a written standard for accuracy, completeness, privacy, and courtesy, coach on the results, and check that reviewers score alike.

elements.title: Survey people after contacts with OMB’s questions
elements.description: For each designated service, ask people after a significant contact, or at the end of the service, whether it increased their trust and what made the difference, using OMB’s Section 280 question wording and response choices.

elements.title: Clear surveys under the Paperwork Reduction Act
elements.description: Get OMB approval before asking the same questions of ten or more people, using the department’s Section 280 umbrella clearance for post-contact surveys where it applies.

elements.title: Report survey data to OMB each quarter
elements.description: For designated services of High Impact Service Providers, send OMB the post-contact survey data by the final business day of January, April, July, and October, for publication on performance.gov.

elements.title: Use what contacts show to improve services
elements.description: Share the top reasons people contact the agency, and where they get stuck, with the program offices and the agency’s service delivery official, so the causes are fixed and not just answered.

elements.title: A Contact Center System Across Phone, Chat, and Email
elements.description: An example architecture: one contact center system takes calls, chats, and emails, routes each to self-service or to an agent with the right skills, offers callbacks, records contacts for quality review, and schedules agents from forecasts, with relay and TTY calls handled like any other.

parts: Toll-free numbers, a phone menu that understands speech and keypresses, and routing by topic, skill, and urgency
Chat on the agency’s website, and email and web forms in the same queues as calls
Callbacks that keep a person’s place in line instead of a long hold
Relay and TTY calls, and a phone menu and voice mail usable with a TTY
Recordings of calls and chats, with evaluation forms for quality review
Forecasts and schedules for agents, and live views of queues and waits
Connections to the contact record, the knowledge base, and the program offices’ case systems
strengths: One place to see every channel’s waits and staff them together
Agents see a person’s earlier contacts, whatever channel they came through
Capacity grows for a surge without new phone lines or equipment
fitsWhen: The center runs on an aging phone system, or on several systems for different channels
Agents work from more than one site, or from home
watchFor: Accessibility has to be tested with relay, TTY, and screen readers, not taken from a product sheet
Recordings and transcripts hold personal information, so who can hear them and how long they’re kept need setting
Moving phone numbers and menus without an outage needs careful planning

elements.title: Contact Records and Handoffs in a CRM
elements.description: An example architecture: each contact is a record in a customer relationship management (CRM) system, with its channel, reason, answer, and outcome, linked to the person’s earlier contacts once they’re verified, and handed to the program office as a case when it must act.

parts: A contact record for each call, chat, email, and web form, with its reason and outcome chosen from set lists
The person’s earlier contacts and open cases, shown once they’re verified
Handoffs that open a case in the program office’s system with the contact’s details, and send the person a reference number
Follow-up tasks and callbacks, with due dates
Retention set from General Records Schedule 6.5, with holds when a contact is part of a dispute
strengths: People don’t have to repeat themselves when they call back or are handed off
Contact reasons recorded the same way show what to fix upstream
Program offices get handoffs with everything they need
fitsWhen: Agents keep notes in spreadsheets, email, or the phone system alone
Handoffs to program offices go by email and are hard to follow up
watchFor: Reason codes only help if there are few enough for agents to choose well, and someone reviews them
A record of every contact about a person is itself sensitive, so access follows role and need

elements.title: One Knowledge Base for Agents, the Website, and Virtual Agents
elements.description: An example architecture: approved answers are written once in a knowledge base, each with an owner in the program office and a review date, and published to agents’ screens, the agency’s website, the phone menu, and virtual agents.

parts: Answers written in plain language, each with its owner, its sources, and its next review date
Review and approval by the program office before an answer is published or changed
Search for agents, with answers suggested from the contact’s topic
Publishing to the website, and to the phone menu and virtual agents, from the same answer
Feedback from agents and the public on answers that are wrong or unclear, routed to the owner
Versions of each answer, so the center can show what it told people on a given day
strengths: People get the same answer on every channel
A change made once reaches agents and the website together
New agents become useful sooner
fitsWhen: Agents keep their own notes or search shared drives for answers
The website and the center give different answers to the same question
watchFor: Answers go stale unless program offices own them and reviews happen on time
Each language the agency serves doubles the work of keeping answers current

elements.title: A Virtual Agent That Answers from Approved Content and Hands Off to People
elements.description: An example architecture: a virtual agent on the website and in the phone menu answers general questions only from the agency’s approved answers, shows where each answer came from, and hands the person to an agent, with the conversation so far, whenever it can’t help or they ask for a person.

parts: A chat window on the website and speech in the phone menu, both usable with assistive technology
Answers drawn only from the approved knowledge base, with a link to the source
Handoff to a live agent at any point, carrying the conversation so far
Verified tasks, such as checking a status, only after the person signs in or is verified
Review of conversations the virtual agent couldn’t answer, and of a sample of those it did
A listing in the agency’s AI use case inventory, and the practices OMB requires if the use is high-impact
strengths: Answers routine questions at any hour without a wait
Agents have more time for people who need them
Questions it can’t answer show where the knowledge base falls short
fitsWhen: Many contacts are general questions with set answers
The knowledge base is current and owned
watchFor: Answers can be wrong or sound surer than they are, so it stays within approved content and is checked over time
It mustn’t decide anyone’s access to a benefit; uses that do are presumed high-impact under OMB’s AI memo
People who can’t or won’t use it need an easy way to reach a person
What people type may include personal information, so where it’s processed and kept matters

elements.title: Caller Verification with One-Time Codes and Signed-In Sessions
elements.description: An example architecture: before an agent discusses a person’s records, the person is verified by a one-time code sent to contact details already on file, or by arriving from a session where they signed in to the agency’s website, and the method used is recorded on the contact.

parts: Levels of verification set for each kind of request, from none for general questions to stronger checks for changes
One-time codes sent by text or email to contact details already on file, never to details the caller gives
Handoffs from a signed-in website session into chat or a callback, carrying who the person is
Knowledge questions only as a fallback, with their limits understood
The method used, and its result, recorded on the contact
strengths: Agents follow the same steps every time, without judgment calls
Codes and signed-in sessions are harder to fake than questions anyone could look up
The record shows how each person was verified, if a disclosure is questioned
fitsWhen: Agents verify people with questions such as date of birth and address
People sign in to the agency’s website for its services
watchFor: Contact details on file can be out of date, so there needs to be another way for people who can’t receive a code
Callers using relay services need a way to verify that works for them
Social engineering targets agents directly, so they need training and the backing to say no

elements.title: AI Summaries, Suggested Answers, and Contact Insights
elements.description: An example architecture: calls and chats are transcribed, and an AI model, in an environment the agency approves, summarizes each one for the record, suggests knowledge articles to the agent, finds the top reasons people contact the agency, and flags contacts worth a quality review, with staff deciding what to do with each.

parts: Transcripts of calls and chats, kept with the recording on the same schedule
A draft summary of each contact that the agent checks and saves
Suggested knowledge articles shown to the agent during the contact
Contact reasons and trends across all contacts, by program and channel
Contacts flagged for quality review, such as long holds or repeat contacts, for reviewers to score
strengths: Agents spend less time on notes and more on people
Trends across every contact, not just a sample, show what to fix upstream
Reviewers spend their time on the contacts most worth reviewing
fitsWhen: Agents’ notes are thin or inconsistent
Managers want to know why people contact the agency, beyond reason codes
watchFor: Summaries and suggestions can be wrong, so agents check each one and accuracy is reviewed over time
Transcripts hold personal information, so where they’re processed and kept matters
The agency’s AI governance may require a listing in its AI use case inventory first

elements.title: Post-Contact Surveys on OMB’s Section 280 Questions
elements.description: An example architecture: after a contact, the person is offered a short survey by text, email, or at the end of a chat or call, using OMB’s Section 280 questions under the department’s umbrella clearance, with results joined to the contact’s channel and reason and sent to OMB each quarter.

parts: A survey offered after the contact, or at the end of the service, on the channel the person used
OMB’s trust question and drivers, with their wording and response choices
An approval under the department’s Section 280 umbrella clearance
Results joined to the contact’s channel, reason, and team, without identifying the person in reports
Quarterly datasets in OMB’s format, sent by the final business day of January, April, July, and October
strengths: Results can be compared with other agencies’ on performance.gov
Joined to contact reasons, the answers show which topics and channels need work
Quarterly reporting comes from the same data the center uses
fitsWhen: The agency is a High Impact Service Provider, or wants results it can compare
The center has no survey, or one with its own questions
watchFor: Response rates are low and skew toward strong feelings, so results need context
Surveys outside the umbrella clearance’s terms need their own Paperwork Reduction Act approval

elements.title: Contact Center Performance Reporting
elements.description: An example architecture: a reporting workspace brings together queue and wait figures, contact records, survey results, and self-service sessions, and shows managers and program offices how each channel is doing, why people contact the agency, and where they get stuck.

parts: Regular feeds from the contact center system, the contact records, the surveys, and the website and virtual agent
Waits, abandonment, and resolution by channel, program, and hour, against the center’s standards
Top contact reasons and repeat contacts, by program
Self-service sessions that ended in a call, and why
Views for program offices of the contacts about their programs
strengths: One set of figures for managers, program offices, and reports to OMB
Program offices see the questions their programs cause
Forecasts and staffing start from real volumes
fitsWhen: Reports are put together by hand each month from several systems
Program offices rarely hear what the center learns
watchFor: Figures defined differently across systems, such as when a contact counts as resolved, need agreeing first
Averages hide the worst hours and channels, so look at the spread too

elements.title: Fifteen Plays of Our Contact Center Approach
elements.description: A 2020 playbook for agencies modernizing their contact centers, in fifteen plays from inventorying every center and number through workforce, cost, and maturity assessments, a shared knowledge base, new technology, and the contracting model, with a downloadable PDF.

attributes.by: Contact Center Center of Excellence, General Services Administration

elements.title: Contact center technologies
elements.description: What each common contact center technology does, from automatic call distributors, intelligent routing, and phone menus to web chat, email response, knowledge management, TTY services, and workforce management.

elements.title: Contact Center Community
elements.description: A community of practice for people who run government contact centers at every level of government, with a mailing list and events on performance, experience, and efficiency. Joining takes a government email address.

elements.title: Customer feedback data handbook
elements.description: The Section 280 post-transaction survey explained, with the trust question, the drivers and their wording, the response scales, how trust is scored, and the data published on performance.gov.

attributes.by: Performance.gov, Office of Management and Budget and General Services Administration

elements.title: Section508.gov
elements.description: Guidance, training, and tools for making technology accessible under Section 508, including how to test, how to write accessibility into a solicitation, and the annual Section 508 assessment.

attributes.by: Office of Government-wide Policy, General Services Administration

elements.title: Plain language guide series
elements.description: How to write, design, and test content people can understand, carried forward from PlainLanguage.gov, for anyone writing the answers agents and the website give.

elements.title: Creating a blueprint for quality: How the PX Contact Center helps agents grow their skills
elements.description: How USAGov’s Public Experience contact center reviews calls and chats, through live monitoring and audits of recordings, coaches agents on what it finds, and holds weekly calibration so reviewers score alike.

elements.title: A cloud contact center product
elements.description: A cloud contact center product with a FedRAMP authorization, configured and run by the agency’s own center.

strengths: The agency controls its menus, routing, and data
New channels and features arrive with the product’s updates
fitsWhen: The agency has people who can configure and run it
watchFor: Another product to buy, secure, and keep up, with its own authorization to operate

elements.title: The department’s shared contact center platform
elements.description: A contact center platform the department runs for its components, with each program getting its own numbers, menus, queues, and reports.

strengths: Uses contracts, skills, and security approvals the department already has
Calls can be passed between components without the person calling again
fitsWhen: The department already runs a platform like this for other components
watchFor: Changes and upgrades are decided for the whole department, not for the program

elements.title: A contact center run by a contractor
elements.description: A contractor provides the agents, the system, and the sites, under service levels the agency sets and monitors.

strengths: The agency can add agents for a surge without hiring
The contractor brings systems and experience running large centers
fitsWhen: Contacts swing widely through the year, such as around deadlines
The agency lacks the staff to run a center itself
watchFor: The agency still owns the answers, the data, and the results, and needs people who can manage the contract well
Contact records, recordings, and the knowledge base must stay the agency’s, and be easy to move at the contract’s end

elements.title: The agency’s shared case platform
elements.description: Contact records, handoffs, and follow-up built on the low-code or CRM platform the agency already runs for its cases.

strengths: Handoffs become cases on the same platform the program offices use
Uses licenses, skills, and security approvals the agency already has
fitsWhen: The program offices already work their cases on the platform
watchFor: The connection to the contact center system, to open records as calls arrive, takes real building

elements.title: The contact center product’s own records
elements.description: The contact records and case features that come with the contact center product.

strengths: Works with calls, chats, and recordings with little building
fitsWhen: Most contacts are resolved by the center without a program office
watchFor: Handoffs to program offices’ own systems still need connecting

elements.title: A knowledge management product
elements.description: A knowledge management product connected to the contact center system and the website.

strengths: Built for review cycles, versions, and publishing to several channels
fitsWhen: The center has many topics or many programs
watchFor: Another product to buy and keep up, and to connect to the website

elements.title: Knowledge articles on the agency’s shared platform
elements.description: Knowledge articles kept on the CRM or case platform the agency already runs.

strengths: Agents find answers on the same screen as the contact record
fitsWhen: The center already works on the platform
watchFor: Publishing to the website and virtual agents may need building

elements.title: The contact center product’s virtual agent
elements.description: The virtual agent that comes with the contact center product, configured to use the agency’s knowledge base.

strengths: Hands off to agents with the conversation, with little building
fitsWhen: The agency runs a contact center product that includes one
watchFor: Its AI model and where it runs need the agency’s approval

elements.title: An AI model the agency approves
elements.description: A virtual agent built on an AI model in an environment the agency has approved, connected to the knowledge base and the contact center.

strengths: The same approved model can serve other uses in the agency
fitsWhen: The agency has an approved AI environment and people who can build on it
watchFor: Handoffs to agents, and testing with assistive technology, take real building

elements.title: Codes and sign-in combined with the contact center
elements.description: The contact center system’s verification steps, combined with a one-time code service and the agency’s public sign-in.

strengths: Uses the sign-in the public already has with the agency
fitsWhen: The agency’s public sign-in and contact center can exchange who a person is
watchFor: Each connection between sign-in, codes, and the contact center needs keeping up

elements.title: The contact center product’s AI features
elements.description: Transcription, summaries, suggested answers, and analytics that come with the contact center product.

strengths: Works with the product’s recordings and queues with little building
fitsWhen: The agency runs a contact center product that includes them
watchFor: Its AI model and where it runs need the agency’s approval

elements.title: An AI model the agency approves
elements.description: Transcripts sent to an AI model in an environment the agency has approved, with results written back to the contact record and reports.

strengths: The same approved model can serve other uses in the agency
fitsWhen: The agency has an approved AI environment and people who can build on it
watchFor: Connections to recordings, contact records, and reports take real building

elements.title: GSA’s Touchpoints
elements.description: GSA’s Touchpoints, a government tool for customer feedback forms, set up for the Section 280 questions and the quarterly reporting to OMB.

strengths: Built for the Section 280 questions and quarterly reporting
Run by GSA for federal agencies, with a FIPS moderate rating on cloud.gov
fitsWhen: The center can link to a survey from its texts, emails, and chat
watchFor: Joining results to contact reasons needs the contact’s details passed to the survey

elements.title: The contact center product’s surveys
elements.description: The survey features of the contact center product, set up with OMB’s questions.

strengths: Surveys can be offered at the end of a call or chat, and joined to the contact automatically
fitsWhen: The agency runs a contact center product with surveys
watchFor: Quarterly datasets still need putting into OMB’s format

elements.title: A reporting workspace
elements.description: Data from the center’s systems brought together in the agency’s analytics tools.

strengths: Reports can join data from every system the center uses
fitsWhen: The agency has analytics tools and people who use them
watchFor: Each feed needs keeping up as the systems change
